title: Corbin and the Carnival Mix-Up
markdown:
The Whisperwind Canal moved in gentle gurgles and sleepy sighs, a blue ribbon through meadows dotted with buttercups and old gnarled trees that had never been in a hurry. Time there took the water's advice. Narrowboats nosed past like polite rumours. On the slightly peeling turquoise roof of a workshop perched Corbin, a crow who acted as station master to the traffic and took the job so earnestly his crest stood up like a small anxious crown. He polished the perch on Tuesdays as if the canal's honour depended on shine, and he noted arrivals in a ledger that had never once been late for its own ink. Black feathers took the sun seriously. His eyes missed little, except, on most days, his own competence.

He hated being wrong. The thought moved through his wing feathers like a draft. So when the Canal Craft Carnival arrived in his head one bright afternoon, he announced it with all the fanfare a crow can muster when he has no plan: hopeful squawks, a chest puffed on credit.

"Jun!" He dropped to the towpath, where his dog friend basked in a loyal patch of sun. Jun's shaggy ears could droop or rise; today they rose. "Tomorrow. The Canal Craft Carnival. Grand."

Jun blinked, considering grand as a flavour. "Grand. And what happens? Will there be sausages?"

"Crafts. Wonderful crafts. Carnival things. Music. Merriment. The finest canal-based artistry." A wing waved at the water, which did not take notes.

Jun's whiskers trembled. Corbin felt the old moth against the glass: specifics, questions, the discovery that he did not know how to organise a carnival. He imagined disappointed faces. His beak went dry. Jun, who understood weather better than schedules, only wagged, a slow thump on worn planks.

"Crafts and music. Splendid." No probe. Steadfast as a mooring.

Under a particularly sturdy weeping willow, Henrietta the hedgehog sat in a nest of her own making and wove reeds and delicate twigs into a miniature boat with the precision of someone who believes every word she hears. Canal Craft Carnival reached her on the breeze. She paused, nose ticking, brow a neat fold. Carnival meant dancing, singing, a rather spectacular parade, elaborate floats, a brass band, lanterns along the cut, fireworks that would be remembered, finest attire. She imagined the water sparkling and everyone arriving as if invited by a poster. She tied off a final reed, a tiny smile of anticipation, and set the little boat on a flat stone to dry.

Morning arrived not with the organised excitement Corbin had vaguely hired, but with an obvious mild confusion, the sort that smells of damp rope and good intentions. He stood on the workshop roof, crest doing a nervous semaphore, left-right, as if signalling a lock that would not open. A duck asked him something and he answered tomorrow, which was not a useful lock-time. Henrietta came along the towpath with her reedy bouquet held aloft, looking for a designated stage and, ideally, an orchestra. Gwynfor the badger, who had heard Canal Carnival Craft in an order that rearranged the day, arrived with polished juggling pins clutched under one arm, ready for the Three-Pin Pirouette and any other dazzling thing his wrists remembered.

"Corbin!" Gwynfor boomed across the water and nearly introduced himself to a mooring rope. "Ready for the carnival craft? I've warmed up."

"Carnival craft?" Corbin's voice climbed a register it did not own. "No. A craft carnival. Things you make. Hands."

"Oh." Gwynfor's grin faltered at the pins. "I've brought my finest juggling. Balancing these is quite a craft." A pin caught the sun, unapologetic.

Henrietta trotted in, bouquet dignified. "Is the band ready? These are for the floral arrangement. The grand musical finale. Such a lovely idea."

Corbin's stomach performed a somersault without a licence. Musical finale. Juggling. Reeds as decoration. Feathers wilted like a forgotten flower on a locker lid. Expectant faces, three different days stacked in one morning, none of them the day he had failed to invent. He wanted the deepest wood, a place with no towpath and no announcements. Postpone sat on his tongue, small and damp. "Perhaps," he began, a puff of air, "we should… postpone. Yes. All of it." His crest drooped. The ledger in his head closed itself.

Jun's wet nose found his leg. "Or we make the best of it. Still a carnival. A different kind. Still crafts. Your organising, such as it is. Gwynfor's juggling. Henrietta's… whatever this splendid hedge is." Ears wiggled.

Corbin looked at them. Anticipation, not a trial. He remembered the quiet of a sturdy nest, the ridiculous joy of a good worm, the fact of making. On his perch waited a small brass button, years old, polished to a religion of order. He took it. The taking cost something.

"This button," he said, hopping down with a flap that meant to be confident, offering it to Henrietta, "was the start of something perfectly ordered. Perhaps some things do not need that to be wonderful." He tossed it. Sun made a brief star of the spin.

"Gwynfor. Your juggling is a craft of skill. Henrietta. The reeds are beautiful. Improvised performances. An Improvised Carnival Craft Extravaganza."

The day, which had been three arguments, became a gathering. Word moved faster than a lock gate. Gwynfor, unbothered by the missing formal stage, sent pins in a blur against the vast blue; they wove light and motion until canal folk gasped as if they had paid and brought a programme. A pin climbed, hung, came home to a paw that knew its job. Henrietta, hearing clap and hubbub, and inspired despite the vanished brass band, tapped her bouquet against a nearby post until the reeds found a rhythm. Ducklings quacked along, unofficial chorus. The brass button, tucked into the weave, winked whenever the sun approved. Other dwellers, seeing that the day had decided to happen, fetched what they had: a carved wooden duck that seemed to smile, a brightly knitted tea-cosy with a cheerful expression it had not been asked for, a painting of the canal that looked like home on a good day, a coil of rope tied into a rose by someone who could not juggle and would not be left out.

Sun on black feathers. Scent of damp reed and excited animals. The distant cheerful babble used the water as a hall. The mix-ups, instead of a verdict, had started things. Corbin watched from the towpath now, not the roof: Gwynfor's last flourish, Henrietta's happy clatter, Jun's tail keeping a private time. He did not deliver a speech about competence or heart or the architecture of improvisation. He felt planks under his feet and the fact that the carnival had occurred, grand in the way a well-built narrowboat is grand: not by towering masts or ornate carvings, by holding, by going, by letting people aboard.

Evening laid gold on the canal. His crest sat down. He cleared his throat.

"Well done. A magnificent Canal Craft Carnival." The words carried. He looked at Jun, at the hedgehog, at the badger with pins at rest, and the smile on his beak had no invoice attached. "Next year," he added, because hope is also a craft, "we shall be even more confused, on purpose." The thought of being wrong drifted off with a moorhen and did not come back for the night.
characters: Corbin (earnest crow station master), Jun (dog friend), Gwynfor (juggling badger)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
